blogs.title: Kohima & Khonoma: Handwoven Loramhoushu Shawls, Cane Kophi Baskets & Stone Craft
blogs.productsHighlighted: Loramhoushu Shawl, Kophi Cane & Bamboo Baskets, Carved Stone Monoliths
blogs.author: Kevino Meyase • Khonoma Artisan Guild
blogs.story: In the stone-paved alleys of Khonoma and Kohima, Angami elders weave intricate 'Kophi' carrying baskets from seasoned mountain cane and split bamboo during the post-harvest months. Alongside basketry, Angami women use traditional backstrap loin looms to weave the iconic 'Loramhoushu' and 'Lohe' shawls featuring striking red, yellow, and green bands over crisp white or black cotton.

comments.text: Bought an authentic Kophi basket directly from Semoma Khel in Khonoma last week—incredible craftsmanship!

blogs.title: Mokokchung Heritage: Ao Naga Tsungkotepsu Warrior Shawls & Organic Rock Honey
blogs.productsHighlighted: Tsungkotepsu Shawl, Bamboo Drinking Mugs, Organic Cliff Honey
blogs.author: Toshi Jamir • Ungma Cultural Weaver
blogs.story: Mokokchung—the cultural heartland of the Ao Naga tribe—is renowned for the 'Tsungkotepsu' shawl. Across its central white median strip, artisans hand-paint symbolic motifs of the mithun, hornbill, tiger, spear, and rooster using natural black tree-sap dye. Visitors to Ungma and Longkhum villages can also pick up smoked bamboo mugs and pure wild rock-bee honey harvested from cliffside forests.

comments.text: Ungma village weavers gladly explain every symbol on the Tsungkotepsu median strip!

blogs.title: Mon & Longwa: Konyak Brass Smithery, Multi-Strand Glass Beadwork & Dao Craft
blogs.productsHighlighted: Konyak Brass Figurines, Multi-Strand Glass Bead Necklaces, Hand-Forged Naga Dao
blogs.author: Wangpha Konyak • Longwa Heritage Collective
blogs.story: High on the Indo-Myanmar ridge at Longwa and Chui villages in Mon District, Konyak blacksmiths and bead-makers preserve centuries-old metallurgy and ornament crafting. Using lost-wax casting, artisans forge brass pendants and ceremonial bells, while women string vibrant red, yellow, and green glass beads into chest ornaments. Master smiths also temper traditional Naga 'Dao' machetes with dyed goat-hair hilts.

blogs.title: Phek District: GI-Tagged Chakhesang Shawls & Himalayan Nettle-Fiber (Thüvü) Weaves
blogs.productsHighlighted: GI-Tagged Chakhesang Shawls, Thüvü (Stinging Nettle) Eco-Textiles
blogs.author: Neingupeu Ritse • Chizami Women Weavers
blogs.story: Awarded the prestigious Geographical Indication (GI) tag, Chakhesang shawls from Phek District feature bold spearhead and diamond geometric motifs symbolizing courage and harmony with nature. In villages like Chizami and Pfutsero, weavers also harvest wild Himalayan stinging nettle ('Thüvü'), boiling and spinning the bark fibers by hand into breathable, organic shawls, jackets, and tote bags.

blogs.title: Wokha & Zunheboto: Lotha Opvuram, Sumi Avakhu Textiles & Artisanal Axone Cakes
blogs.productsHighlighted: Lotha Opvuram & Sumi Avakhu Shawls, Pineapple Preserves, Fermented Axone Cakes
blogs.author: Yingbemo Patton & Kivi Zhimomi
blogs.story: Travelling through Wokha (Lotha tribe) and neighbouring Zunheboto (Sumi tribe) rewards visitors with both prestigious handlooms—such as the Lotha 'Opvuram' and Sumi 'Avakhu' textiles—and Nagaland's finest highland pantry staples. Roadside co-ops around Doyang and Baghty valley offer sun-ripened pineapple and passionfruit preserves, while Zunheboto homesteads wrap smoky, umami-rich fermented soybean ('Axone') cakes in banana leaves.
